questions.q: Now that scammers use AI, how should you judge whether a message might be a scam?
options: By whether it contains spelling and grammar mistakes
By how professional and polished the message looks
By whether it uses your name and personal details
By what it asks for, like urgency, secrecy or gift cards
questions.explain: AI lets scammers write polished, personalized messages, so bad spelling is no longer a giveaway. Urgency, secrecy, payment by gift card, wire transfer or crypto, or a "verify your account" link are red flags however professional it looks.

questions.q: You get a panicked call that sounds exactly like your grandchild, asking for money urgently. What should you do?
options: Send the money quickly, since the voice is clearly theirs
Hang up and call back on a number you already know
Ask the caller to text you a new number to confirm it's them
Stay on the line and ask for the details of where to send it
questions.explain: Scammers can clone a voice from a short recording. If a call feels urgent and unusual, hang up and call back on a number you already know, and agree on a family code word ahead of time.

questions.q: You want AI's help replying to a client, and the email thread includes their name and contract figures. What should you do?
options: Describe it instead, using "my client" and rounded numbers
Paste the full thread, since AI needs every detail to help
Paste it, then delete the chat so it's gone everywhere
Avoid AI entirely, since it can never help with work email
questions.explain: You can almost always get the same help by swapping specifics for descriptions, like "my client" instead of a name and rounded numbers instead of exact figures. Deleting a chat doesn't mean it's gone everywhere.
